blocks.text: K. wondered whether he ought not to leave with all possible haste; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect of his being able to do so during the sermon, he would then have to remain as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long since ceased to be under any obligation to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was eleven. But could a sermon really be about to be preached? Could K. alone constitute the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who merely wished to see the church? At bottom he was nothing else. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at eleven o’clock, on a weekday in the most dreadful weather. The priest—a priest he undoubtedly was, a young man with a smooth, dark face—was evidently only going up to extinguish the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

But this was not so, the priest instead examined the light and turned it up a little more, then slowly turned towards the parapet, which he grasped with both hands at the front of its angular rim. Thus he stood for a while and looked about without moving his head. K. had retreated a considerable distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw the verger somewhere, without being able to make out precisely where, crouching down with bent back, peacefully, as though his task were done. What stillness now reigned in the cathedral! But K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of remaining here; if it was the priest’s duty to preach at a particular hour regardless of the circumstances, then let him do so, he would succeed even without K.’s assistance, just as K.’s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. So K. slowly set off, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then reached the broad central aisle and walked there too quite unmolested, save that the stone floor rang beneath the lightest footfall and the vaults echoed it faintly but unceasingly, in manifold, regular progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked there alone between the empty pews, perhaps watched by the priest, and the size of the cathedral seemed to him to lie at the very limit of what human beings could still endure. When he reached his former place, he fairly snatched up the album he had left lying there, without lingering further, and took it with him. He had almost left the pews behind and was approaching the open space between them and the exit when he heard the priest’s voice for the first time. A powerful, practised voice. How it penetrated the cathedral, which stood ready to receive it! But it was not the congregation the priest was calling to, it was quite unambiguous and there was no evading it, he called: “Josef K.!”

K. stopped short and looked at the floor before him. For the present he was still free, he could still walk on and make his escape through one of the three small dark wooden doors not far ahead of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that, though he had understood, he did not wish to concern himself with it. But if he turned round, he was caught, for then he would have admitted that he had understood quite well, that he really was the person being called and that he was also willing to obey. Had the priest called again, K. would certainly have gone away, but since everything remained silent, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little after all, for he wished to see what the priest was doing now. He stood quietly in the pulpit as before, but it was plain to see that he had noticed K.’s turn of the head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned completely round. He did so and was beckoned nearer by a motion of the priest’s finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran—he did so also out of curiosity and to shorten the affair—with long, flying strides towards the pulpit. He halted by the first pews, but the distance still seemed too great to the priest, who stretched out his hand and, with his forefinger pointing sharply downwards, indicated a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too, at this spot he already had to bend his head far back to keep the priest in view. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, raising one hand from the parapet in an indefinite gesture. “Yes,” said K., he thought of how openly he had always given his name before, for some time now it had been a burden to him, and now people whom he was meeting for the first time already knew his name; how pleasant it was to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You are accused,” said the priest very softly. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of it.” “Then you are the man I am looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “Oh, I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the priest, “to speak to you.” “I did not know,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian round the cathedral.” “Leave aside what is incidental,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” replied K., “it is an album of the sights of the town.” “Put it down,” said the priest. K. flung it away so violently that it fell open and slid some distance across the floor with its pages crumpled. “Do you know that your case is going badly?” asked the priest. “It seems so to me too,” said K. “I have made every effort, but so far without success. Admittedly, I have not yet finished the petition.” “How do you imagine it will end,” asked the priest. “Formerly I thought it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. You are held to be guilty. Your case may never get beyond a lower court. For the present, at least, your guilt is held to be proved.” “But I am not guilty,” said K. “It is a mistake. How can a human being be guilty at all. We are all human beings here, one like another.” “That is true,” said the priest, “but that is how the guilty are wont to speak.” “Are you too prejudiced against me?” asked K. “I am not prejudiced against you,” said the priest. “I thank you,” said K. “But all the others who are concerned in the proceedings are prejudiced against me. They instil it into those who are not concerned as well. My position is becoming more and more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest. “The judgement does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually pass into judgement.” “So that is how it is,” said K., lowering his head. “What do you intend to do next about your case?” asked the priest. “I intend to seek further help,” said K., raising his head to see what the priest thought of this. “There are still certain possibilities I have not made use of.” “You seek too much help from others,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and particularly from women. Do you not see that it is not the true help.” “Sometimes, and indeed often, I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could persuade a few women I know to work together on my behalf, I should be bound to succeed. Particularly with this court, which consists almost entirely of woman-chasers. Show the examining magistrate a woman in the distance and he will run over the court table and the accused simply to get there in time.” The priest bowed his head towards the parapet, only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to weigh down upon him. What a storm might be raging outside? This was no longer a dull day, it was already the dead of night. None of the stained glass in the great windows could break the dark wall with so much as a glimmer. And just now the verger began extinguishing the candles on the high altar one after another. “Are you angry with me,” K. asked the priest. “Perhaps you do not know what sort of court you serve.” He received no answer. “These are merely my own experiences,” said K. Above him all remained silent. “I did not mean to offend you,” said K. Then the priest shouted down to K.: “Can you not see two steps before you?” It was shouted in anger, but at the same time as though by someone who sees another fall and, being frightened himself, cries out heedlessly and involuntarily.
